CHAPTER XLVII. THE “ENDLESS ENDING”

As yet I have not found Lona, but Mara is much with me. She has taught
me many things, and is teaching me more.

Can it be that that last waking also was in the dream? that I am still
in the chamber of death, asleep and dreaming, not yet ripe enough to
wake? Or can it be that I did not go to sleep outright and heartily,
and so have come awake too soon? If that waking was itself but a dream,
surely it was a dream of a better waking yet to come, and I have not
been the sport of a false vision! Such a dream must have yet lovelier
truth at the heart of its dreaming!

In moments of doubt I cry,

“Could God Himself create such lovely things as I dreamed?”

“Whence then came thy dream?” answers Hope.

“Out of my dark self, into the light of my consciousness.”

“But whence first into thy dark self?” rejoins Hope.

“My brain was its mother, and the fever in my blood its father.”

“Say rather,” suggests Hope, “thy brain was the violin whence it issued,
and the fever in thy blood the bow that drew it forth.--But who made
the violin? and who guided the bow across its strings? Say rather,
again--who set the song birds each on its bough in the tree of life, and
startled each in its order from its perch? Whence came the fantasia? and
whence the life that danced thereto? Didst THOU say, in the dark of thy
own unconscious self, ‘Let beauty be; let truth seem!’ and straightway
beauty was, and truth but seemed?”

Man dreams and desires; God broods and wills and quickens.

When a man dreams his own dream, he is the sport of his dream; when
Another gives it him, that Other is able to fulfil it.

I have never again sought the mirror. The hand sent me back: I will not
go out again by that door! “All the days of my appointed time will I
wait till my change come.”

Now and then, when I look round on my books, they seem to waver as if
a wind rippled their solid mass, and another world were about to break
through. Sometimes when I am abroad, a like thing takes place; the
heavens and the earth, the trees and the grass appear for a moment to
shake as if about to pass away; then, lo, they have settled again into
the old familiar face! At times I seem to hear whisperings around me, as
if some that loved me were talking of me; but when I would distinguish
the words, they cease, and all is very still. I know not whether these
things rise in my brain, or enter it from without. I do not seek them;
they come, and I let them go.

Strange dim memories, which will not abide identification, often,
through misty windows of the past, look out upon me in the broad
daylight, but I never dream now. It may be, notwithstanding, that, when
most awake, I am only dreaming the more! But when I wake at last into
that life which, as a mother her child, carries this life in its bosom,
I shall know that I wake, and shall doubt no more.

I wait; asleep or awake, I wait.

Novalis says, “Our life is no dream, but it should and will perhaps
become one.”




     *Chapter 42: William Law.

     **Chapter 45: Tin tin sonando con sì dolce nota
                   Che ‘l ben disposto spirito d’ amor turge.
                                        DEL PARADISO, x. 142.

     ***Chapter 46: Oma’ vedrai di sì fatti uficiali.
                                        Del Purgatorio, ii. 30.

Is it possible that the waking I believed to be real was itself only a dream? That I remain in the chamber of death, asleep, dreaming—not yet ready to awaken fully? Or perhaps I never truly surrendered to sleep, and so stirred awake too soon, before the time was right?

If that awakening was but a dream, then it must have been a dream of a greater awakening yet to come—a vision pointing toward a truth more radiant than any I have known. Such a dream cannot be false; it must contain within its very fabric a deeper reality, a lovelier truth pulsing beneath the surface of illusion.

When doubt creeps in, I cry aloud: *“Could God Himself fashion such beauty as I dreamed?”*
And Hope answers: *“Whence then came thy dream?”*
*“From my own darkness,”* I reply, *“into the light of consciousness.”*
But Hope persists: *“Then where did that darkness first receive the seed?”*
*“My brain gave birth to it,”* I say, *“and the fever in my blood fathered it.”*
*“Say rather,”* Hope suggests gently, *“that your brain was the violin, and the fever the bow that drew the music from its strings.”*
But then I pause—*“Who crafted the violin? Who guided the bow? Who placed each bird upon its bough in the tree of life, and startled it into song in perfect order?”*
*“Whence came the fantasia?”* I ask. *“And whence the life that danced to its rhythm?”*
Did I, deep in the silence of my unconscious self, whisper: *“Let beauty be; let truth seem”*—and at once, beauty bloomed, while truth wore only the semblance of being?

Man dreams and desires.
God broods, wills, and brings forth life.
When a man dreams his own dream, he is captive to its shape. But when another gives him the dream—the One who knows its end—he can trust it to unfold as it should.

I no longer seek the mirror. The hand that sent me back shall not find me returning through that door. I will not go out again by the way I came.
*“All the days of my appointed time,”* I say, *“I will wait until my change comes.”*

Sometimes, when I look upon my books, they waver—as if a hidden wind stirs their solid forms, and another world presses close behind. At times, when I walk outside, the sky and earth tremble, the trees and grass blur for an instant, as though all things were about to dissolve. Then, just as quickly, they settle—returning to their familiar shapes, as if nothing had changed.

Yet I hear whispers now—soft voices, like lovers speaking of me in hushed tones. When I turn, they vanish. No words remain. Only silence, thick and profound.
Are these echoes born within me, or do they drift in from some other realm? I do not chase them. They come unbidden, and I let them pass.

Strange memories flicker—shadows of moments I cannot name—appearing through misty windows of the past, even in broad daylight. But I no longer dream. Not in the old way.

Still—perhaps the moment I feel most awake, I am dreaming the deepest of all.

But when I finally awaken into that life which cradles this one as a mother holds her child, I will know. I will know with certainty. And then there will be no doubt.

I wait.
Whether asleep or awake, I wait.

Novalis once said: *“Our life is no dream—but it should and will perhaps become one.”*
